correspondence.component_scope: Headward opening and upper North Anna approach
finding: The selected opening lies on the mapped Mountain Run corridor beside Gordonsville Municipal Airport. The original map follows it northeast and then east/southeast, receiving Madison Run, toward the Negro Run junction setting.

Mountain Run is separately labeled. Below the junction setting, the selected corridor is labeled North Anna River. White Oak Creek is a distinct north-side feeder; the mapped North Anna continues toward Vawter Corner and the head of the western Lake Anna arm.
The headward route is read directly on original cartography; it is not inferred merely from a nearby label or basin membership.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete at ordinary generalized component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Lake Anna passage and outlet
finding: The selected North Anna approach enters the reservoir from the west, passes the US 522 crossing, and continues through the main Lake Anna waterbody toward its southeast outlet.

The northern Pamunkey Creek arm is depicted separately from the selected western North Anna approach. Its shared word Pamunkey does not make that branch the selected opening or establish one whole-route name.

The Contrary Creek arm and other lateral drowned tributaries join the reservoir. The selected corridor follows the main lake toward the dam/outlet, rather than traversing the enclosed southern cooling-water arms.
Original map continuity covers the reservoir-to-river outlet. Louisa County independently states that North Anna River was dammed to create Lake Anna.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete at ordinary generalized component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Middle and lower North Anna to South Anna confluence
finding: Below the Lake Anna dam/outlet, the map repeatedly labels North Anna River through the county-boundary corridor, past the Hewlett/Noel setting, the Interstate 95 crossing and Doswell/Garnett Crossing area.
The Little River approaches from the west near Little River Crossing. The selected route stays on North Anna rather than extending up Little River.

Farther south, the mapped North Anna and South Anna meet; the downstream channel is labeled Pamunkey River. The selected headward route uses North Anna, with South Anna a distinct receiving-junction branch.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete at ordinary generalized component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper and middle Pamunkey
finding: The named Pamunkey meanders east and southeast from the Anna confluence, through the US 301/Hanover setting to Hanovertown and the US 360 crossing.

The selected route continues past the Horseshoe/Chericoke setting, Putneys Mill and Elsing Green. Direct original map reading follows the whole corridor, with tributary streams and swamp channels shown separately.

Virginia DWR prose independently describes the Pamunkey from the North Anna–South Anna confluence through Hanovertown, the Route 360 crossing and Putneys Mill, and its transition to a widening tidal estuary downstream.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete at ordinary generalized component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower estuarine Pamunkey and actual terminal
finding: The original map follows the broad labeled Pamunkey around the Pamunkey Reservation and Cohoke Marsh, then White Oak Landing, Romancoke and Eltham Marsh toward West Point.
The Mattaponi is mapped as a separate river on the opposite side of West Point. The waters below their meeting are labeled York River.

The selected route ends in the West Point confluence/upper York estuarine setting. It does not select the full downstream York River to Chesapeake Bay or an open-ocean mouth. This observation is at ordinary terminal-corridor scale, not an exact bank or endpoint placement claim.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete at ordinary generalized component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: headward opening and southwestward upper route
correspondence.finding: The northeastern opening and its southwestward course lie east of the central West Greenland coastal mountain/fjord belt, in the mapped continuous Inland Ice. The map’s graticule and regional coastline place the whole headward setting north and east of the Rink outlet corridor.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete at ordinary generalized component/corridor scale.
correspondence.name_observation: No natural-river hydronym is established for this interior opening. Ice-surface contours, thickness isopachs and bedrock contours do not identify a river.

correspondence.component_scope: southwestward continuation and southward middle bend
correspondence.finding: The selected continuation and pronounced southward turn remain within the mapped Inland Ice, inland of the separate northern coastal outlets. Original map coverage includes the whole intermediate setting and joins the upper and lower corridor views without a missing geographic interval.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete at ordinary generalized component/corridor scale.
correspondence.name_observation: No neighboring fjord, glacier or place label is extended over this interior model course.

correspondence.component_scope: long westward lower ice corridor
correspondence.finding: After the southward bend, the selected course trends west through the continental-ice setting toward the coast. The original map shows the ice surface narrowing toward the Rink Isbræ outlet between exposed coastal terrain. This is geographic ice/outlet correspondence, not proof of a surface or subglacial river.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete at ordinary generalized component/corridor scale.
correspondence.name_observation: Rink Isbræ is contextual identification of the glacier approach only; it is not a candidate natural-river hydronym.

correspondence.component_scope: outlet-glacier transition and actual terminal setting
correspondence.finding: The western ending lies at the mapped Rink Isbræ outlet into the inner eastern part of Karrat Isfjord. The terminal view shows exposed land on either side of the ice tongue, the ice-to-fjord transition, and the fjord extending west. This distinguishes the actual inner-fjord terminal from neighboring northern outlets and the outer marine coast.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete at ordinary generalized component/corridor scale.
correspondence.name_observation: Karrat Isfjord is a fjord name. Neither it nor Rink Isbræ supplies a representative river identity for the complete FID.

correspondence.component_scope: Selected glaciated opening and Snow River outlet valley
correspondence.finding: The selected head begins on the mapped continuous glacier/icefield east of the separate Moose Creek valley. The glaciated surface funnels south into the valley whose outwash and braided channel are repeatedly labeled Snow River. The original topography shows the ice tongue opening directly into that channel corridor, so this is more than a nearby river-label association. No surface river line, independent glacier name, current ice front, or exact source point is assigned to the modeled passage over ice. The glaciated opening is not called Kenai River.
correspondence.correspondence: supported_at_component_corridor_scale
correspondence.reading_scope: Original bounded USGSTopo raster pixels and private enlargements/orientation views.

correspondence.component_scope: Snow River beside the Paradise lakes
correspondence.finding: Below the mapped ice tongue, the selection follows the north–south Snow River braid valley and then its southwestward bend through the Paradise Valley setting. Upper Paradise Lake is alongside the eastern side of the corridor; Lower Paradise Lake lies alongside the western side farther downstream. The main Snow River channel is mapped separately from these lakes. They are lateral waters, not selected lake-axis passages, and the generalized model does not establish a separate name for every local braid.
correspondence.correspondence: supported_at_component_corridor_scale
correspondence.reading_scope: Original bounded USGSTopo raster pixels and private enlargements/orientation views.

correspondence.component_scope: Snow River, South Fork junction and southern Kenai Lake inlet
correspondence.finding: The selected southwestward Snow River reaches the low valley northeast of the highway and railway corridor, passes the South Fork Snow River approach from the south/east, and bends north along the combined braid corridor. It passes the Seward Highway crossing and reaches the southern arm of Kenai Lake near Primrose. The south-fork approach is a distinct lateral branch and is not substituted for the selected glacier-fed northern approach.
correspondence.correspondence: supported_at_component_corridor_scale
correspondence.reading_scope: Original bounded USGSTopo raster pixels and private enlargements/orientation views.

correspondence.component_scope: Kenai Lake southern, east–west and northwestern arms
correspondence.finding: The selected route passes north through the southern Kenai Lake arm, turns west along the long central arm, and turns northwest toward the western outlet at Cooper Landing. Mapped Trail River/Trail Creek and Ptarmigan Creek approaches meet the lake on the eastern side; Quartz Creek enters near the northwestern arm. Those tributaries, nearby Trail lakes and Cooper Lake are outside the selected course. The service also repeats Kenai River network labels inside the waterbody; the separately printed Kenai Lake identity and its inlet/outlet geometry are retained. Neither those network labels nor the modeled interior line make the lake a uniformly named river.
correspondence.correspondence: supported_at_component_corridor_scale
correspondence.reading_scope: Original bounded USGSTopo raster pixels and private enlargements/orientation views.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper Kenai River and major tributary junctions
correspondence.finding: At the western end of Kenai Lake the route enters the mapped Kenai River through Cooper Landing. It follows the westward upper river past the Juneau Creek and Cooper Creek side approaches, then the Russian River junction from the south, and continues west past Jean Creek before turning southwest through the canyon/Surprise Creek setting into the northeastern part of Skilak Lake. These connected channels and turns were read on the original map; the route is not inferred merely from shared basin membership.
correspondence.correspondence: supported_at_component_corridor_scale
correspondence.reading_scope: Original bounded USGSTopo raster pixels and private enlargements/orientation views.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern Skilak Lake and fragment transition
correspondence.finding: FID2698 enters the northeastern Skilak Lake margin from upper Kenai River and extends southwest into the lake interior, where the selected fragment changes to FID2699. The Skilak River enters the lake separately from the southeast; it is a lateral inlet and not the selected upper river. The map covers the lake-entry setting, separate inlet and the fragment boundary within the lake.
correspondence.correspondence: supported_at_component_corridor_scale
correspondence.reading_scope: Original bounded USGSTopo raster pixels and private enlargements/orientation views.

correspondence.component_scope: Skilak Lake crossing and northwestern outlet
correspondence.finding: FID2699 continues the modeled westward passage through Skilak Lake and approaches its northwestern Kenai River outlet. The model simplifies the open-water course and the western shoreline/outlet turn; it is assessed at lake-and-outlet-corridor scale, not as exact bank agreement. Original cartography clearly joins the lake to the downstream Kenai River. Hidden Lake and its tributary connection, as well as the Skilak River inlet, are distinct lateral features. No reservoir identity or uniform river name is assigned to the lake.
correspondence.correspondence: supported_at_component_corridor_scale
correspondence.reading_scope: Original bounded USGSTopo raster pixels and private enlargements/orientation views.

correspondence.component_scope: Kenai River below Skilak Lake to Sterling and Soldotna
correspondence.finding: Below Skilak Lake the selected line follows the repeatedly labeled Kenai River, west and northwest past the Killey River side approach, then around the Sterling-area bend at the Moose River junction. It continues southwest past the Funny River junction and through the broader Soldotna corridor, with Soldotna Creek and Slikok Creek as separate lateral approaches. The original views overlap across the lake outlet and this entire lower corridor; the coarse selected line straightens river bends without changing the represented corridor.
correspondence.correspondence: supported_at_component_corridor_scale
correspondence.reading_scope: Original bounded USGSTopo raster pixels and private enlargements/orientation views.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower estuary, Kenai and actual marine terminal
correspondence.finding: From the Soldotna area the selected course continues north and then west through the lower Kenai River corridor past the Beaver Creek junction toward Kenai. The mapped lower river makes large estuarine loops before opening to the coast beside Kenai. The modeled final reach shortcuts these loops and extends into coastal open water near the river-mouth setting; it is not an exact mouth point or present navigable channel. The primary map establishes the actual marine receiving setting, and the earlier-read official plan identifies that receiving water as Cook Inlet. No downstream inland river or lake connector is missing.
correspondence.correspondence: supported_at_component_corridor_scale
correspondence.reading_scope: Original bounded USGSTopo raster pixels and private enlargements/orientation views.

correspondence.component_scope: Western headward river-and-lake setting
correspondence.finding: The western selected opening lies among the small streams and lake expansions in the inland upper Kingora corridor. The original shows the eastward watercourse and multiple short side-stream/lake arms; nearby westward drainage toward the Committee Bay side is separately drawn. The source does not establish an official source boundary or a separate hydronym for the first selected feeder.
correspondence.correspondence: Mapped general setting and eastward river/lake corridor read

correspondence.component_scope: Upper Kingora River and eastern adjoining-sheet continuation
correspondence.finding: The labelled Kingora corridor continues east through elongated unnamed lake expansions, receives distinct southern and northern feeders, and narrows into river and rapid-marked reaches toward the eastern sheet boundary. The adjoining Hall Lake sheet continues this river corridor toward Sarcpa Lake. The larger southern lake arm is a lateral inflow rather than the selected western approach.
correspondence.correspondence: Upper river, elongated lake passages, tributary junctions and cross-sheet continuity read

correspondence.component_scope: Sarcpa Lake and northern outlet chain
correspondence.finding: The western Kingora approach reaches Sarcpa Lake. A separately labelled Saniraq River arrives from the southwest. The selected continuation follows Sarcpa's northern arm and the intervening elongated lake/channel chain into the river's northward bend before it turns east. These are directly depicted water connections; basin membership alone is not used.
correspondence.correspondence: Selected lake passage and northward connection read

correspondence.component_scope: Lower Kingora River and Hall Lake entrance
correspondence.finding: After the northern lake chain, the river turns east and southeast down the incised corridor to the western Hall Lake shore. Side streams and the river's mouth at Hall Lake are mapped. The sheet's C2 fisheries comment independently names the Kingora River mouth beside Hall Lake; this corroborates the observed river component without extending its name over the lake.
correspondence.correspondence: Lower river corridor, side junctions and actual lake entrance read

correspondence.component_scope: Hall Lake passage and northeastern Sarvuq Inlet
correspondence.finding: The selected continuation crosses the broad Hall Lake water body and turns northeast into its Sarvuq Inlet arm. The map shows the northern and western lake arms, islands, other tributary mouths and the eastern shore. These remain lake/inlet components rather than uniformly named Kingora reaches.
correspondence.correspondence: Main lake, material arms and selected northeastern inlet setting read

correspondence.component_scope: Northeastern connector and selected Foster Bay terminal setting
correspondence.finding: The source depicts Sarvuq Inlet, the intervening small-waterbody/coastal terrain and the southwestern Foster Bay coast, but the inspected mapping does not establish a continuous selected inlet-to-coast waterway. The small coastal streams and ponds cannot be assumed to connect back to Sarvuq merely because the retained model reaches the coast. Consequently the actual selected terminal connection remains pending.
correspondence.correspondence: Surrounding lake, coastal ponds/streams and Foster Bay shoreline read; connecting selected waterway not established

correspondence.component_scope: Separately mapped Hall Lake outlet and bounded primary prose
correspondence.finding: Hall Lake's southeastern outlet is labelled Ikerasak River and is mapped through its islanded lower reach into Roche Bay. Fish-resource notes M2, D2 and D3 describe migration between Hall Lake and the Ikerasak outlet and place that river in Roche Bay. This provides bounded drainage context, not correspondence for the selected Sarvuq–Foster ending.
correspondence.correspondence: Alternative actual outlet mapped and corroborated; outside selected northeastern ending
